## Q1 | The Butterbeer Tax

The Ministry of Magic was in some financial trouble after their considerable expenditures during the war. They decided to impose a tax of 6 galleons on the sale of butterbeer as a source of funding. Use a graph to evaluate the welfare effects the policy had on the market. The supply and demand curves for butterbeer can be represented by the following equations.

$$
D: P_B = 40 - Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 10 + \frac{1}{2} Q_S
$$

Use a graph and algebra to calculate equilibrium before and after the tax. Start with the pre-tax equilibrium. Then use the tax equation ($P_B = \tau + P_S$) to solve for equilibrium quantity and the two prices. Conclude with the remaining relevant components. *Note: ~~Like Q1,~~ I’m looking for a complete description of the impacts on the market.*

::::

Who bears more of the tax? *buyers · sellers · equal*

::::: solution

Pre-Tax Price: $20$ galleons. Pre-Tax Quantity: $20$ bottles. Post-Tax Quantity: $16$ bottles. Buyer Price: $24$ galleons. Seller Price: $18$ galleons. Consumer Surplus: $128$. Producer Surplus: $64$. Government Revenue: $96$. Deadweight Loss: $12$. Tax Incidence on Buyers: $4$. Tax Incidence on Sellers: $2$. Who bears more of the tax? Buyers.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Without the tax, buyers and sellers face one price:

$$
40 - Q = 10 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 20, \quad P = 20
$$

Before the tax, consumer surplus is the triangle above $20$, $\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 20 = 200$, and producer surplus the triangle below it, $\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10 = 100$.

With the tax, the buyer price sits $6$ above the seller price, and the market still clears at one quantity. Slide the $6$-galleon wedge in from the left until it gets stuck between the curves:

$$
P_B = 6 + P_S \quad\Rightarrow\quad 40 - Q = 6 + (10 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 16
$$

so $P_B = 40 - 16 = 24$ and $P_S = 10 + 8 = 18$.

:::

::: column

![Tax equilibrium](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Incidence: buyers pay $24 - 20 = 4$ more than before, sellers receive $20 - 18 = 2$ less. Buyers bear more because demand is steeper (less elastic) than supply: buyers are less able to walk away, so more of the tax lands on them.

Welfare: consumer surplus shrinks from the triangle above $20$ to the triangle above $24$, $\frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 16 = 128$; producer surplus from the triangle below $20$ to the one below $18$, $\frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 8 = 64$. The rectangle between the two prices over the $16$ bottles still sold is government revenue, $6 \times 16 = 96$. The triangle between the curves over the $4$ bottles no longer sold is deadweight loss:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (20 - 16) = 12
$$

Check: $200 + 100 = 128 + 64 + 96 + 12$.

:::::

## Q2 | The Butterbeer Subsidy

Now suppose that instead of the tax, the Ministry of Magic pays a 6 galleon subsidy on every butterbeer sold. Use a graph and algebra to discuss the impact of the subsidy on the market. Use the subsidy equation ($P_S = s + P_B$) to solve for equilibrium quantity and the two prices.

::::

For the bottles sold beyond the pre-subsidy quantity, how does marginal benefit compare with marginal cost?

> a\) Marginal benefit is above marginal cost, so these added trades raise total surplus.
>
> b\) Marginal benefit is below marginal cost, so these added trades reduce total surplus once the Ministry’s spending is counted.
>
> c\) Marginal benefit equals marginal cost, so these added trades leave total surplus unchanged.
>
> d\) The subsidy lowers the sellers’ marginal cost, so these added trades cost society nothing.

::::: solution

Post-Subsidy Quantity: $24$ bottles. Buyer Price: $16$ galleons. Seller Price: $22$ galleons. The choice is **b)**.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

A subsidy is the tax wedge turned around: the seller now receives $6$ more than the buyer pays, so the wedge sits to the *right* of the no-policy equilibrium:

$$
P_S = 6 + P_B \quad\Rightarrow\quad 10 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 6 + (40 - Q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 24
$$

so $P_B = 40 - 24 = 16$ and $P_S = 10 + 12 = 22$.

:::

::: column

![Subsidy equilibrium](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Both sides are better off: buyers pay $4$ less and sellers receive $2$ more, so consumer surplus rises from $200$ to $\frac{1}{2} \times 24 \times 24 = 288$ and producer surplus from $100$ to $\frac{1}{2} \times 24 \times 12 = 144$. But the Ministry pays $6 \times 24 = 144$, more than the $(288 - 200) + (144 - 100) = 132$ the buyers and sellers gain. The difference is the deadweight loss, the triangle between the curves over the four added bottles:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (24 - 20) = 12
$$

**b)** Beyond the pre-subsidy $20$ bottles, supply (marginal cost) is above demand (marginal benefit). The $21$st through $24$th bottles cost $20.5$ to $22$ galleons to make, but buyers value them at only $19$ down to $16$; they are made only because the Ministry pays the gap. Counting the Ministry’s spending, each one lowers total surplus, by the $12$ above. Not a): that is the bottles *before* $20$. Not c): marginal benefit equals marginal cost only at $20$. Not d): the subsidy changes who pays the cost, not the cost itself; the Ministry’s galleons are a real cost to society.

:::::
